claims.text: The nanoscale PGM catalyst has outstanding catalytic performance in ethanol oxidation.
Complete ethanol oxidation involves transfer of 12 electrons and 12 protons.
The catalyst's performance is governed by in situ formation of a reactive platinum oxy-hydroxide layer.
The platinum oxy-hydroxide layer modulates the adsorption energies of ethanol and reaction intermediates.
The platinum oxy-hydroxide layer promotes proton-coupled electron transfer.
Promotion of proton-coupled electron transfer by the oxy-hydroxide layer enhances catalytic activity, selectivity, and durability.
Controlled potential cycling induces and regenerates a surface oxy-hydroxide layer.
Holding the catalyst at a constant reducing potential suppresses oxide formation.
Potential cycling periodically forms platinum oxy-hydroxide species on the catalyst surface.
Periodic adsorption-energy modulation facilitates complete ethanol oxidation through proton-coupled electron transfer.
Dynamic oxy-hydroxide formation regenerates active sites, prevents poisoning, and improves durability.
Potential-cycled catalysts will exhibit higher turnover frequencies than catalysts held at constant reducing potential.
Potential-cycled catalysts will produce a higher proportion of CO2 relative to partial oxidation products.
Potential-cycled catalysts will show less surface deactivation and slower activity degradation than the reducing-potential baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies when dynamic oxidation-reduction cycles and reversible oxy-hydroxide formation are feasible.
The proposed mechanism may fail in strongly reducing environments that preclude oxy-hydroxide formation.
The proposed mechanism may fail at very high temperatures where oxy-hydroxide species are unstable.
